title: Tagged render-intent union for tool-call presentation
summary: A tool declares how its call and its result are shown through a tagged union (generic, terminal or diff card) with a required tag, instead of a bag of optional fields.
firstReason: A closed, tagged set of card kinds is easy to express in Go and gives the server-side renderer one switch; keep the model.

title: Prompt variables and tool-guidance ownership
summary: Every fact in the system prompt has exactly one owner: the loop supplies route facts such as the model name as variables, each tool owns its own description and usage guidance, and the persona owns role and behaviour. Prompt assembly takes a per-agent context.
firstReason: Single ownership of prompt facts prevents drift between what the harness knows and what the prompt says; keep it.

title: Tool-call timeout policy as a plugin
summary: Tool-call timeout is a policy plugin: the tool pipeline has an around-dispatch extension point, and the plugin wraps any tool that declares a timeout with a derived cancellation signal. A tool that declares no timeout gets none.
firstReason: An around-dispatch hook plus a policy component is the right shape in Go too, with a derived context carrying the deadline.

title: Cooperative tool cancellation at the registry boundary
summary: Every tool invocation must carry a cancellation signal owned by its caller; the registry supplies no default. Only the around-dispatch stage may replace the signal, for example to add a deadline.
firstReason: This is already the Go convention: a context.Context passed as the first argument, with wrappers deriving child contexts.

title: PTC owns policy-change cleanup waits
summary: Changing a session's permission mode commits immediately. The PTC executor observes the change, cancels affected calls and makes its own next call wait for that cleanup, so permission setters never wait.
firstReason: Making every setter await process cleanup spread one component's lifecycle into unrelated callers. The owner of a slow cleanup absorbs the wait; the same ownership rule suits every Go component that supervises a process.

title: Explicit text and image output in PTC
summary: A `run_code` program chooses what the model sees by calling `inspect(...values)`; text, objects and images appear in one ordered output. The final expression or return value is discarded, so incidental data never reaches the model's context.
firstReason: Explicit output selection is a model-facing contract that keeps intermediate tool results out of the context window. The formatting runs inside the JavaScript program runtime, which stays a separate process, so the Go host only transports the selected output.

title: PTC output truncation without execution cancellation
summary: When a program's captured output exceeds its budget, the runtime keeps an ordered prefix, drops the rest and sets `outputTruncated`; it does not cancel the program or discard retained variables. A truncated failure keeps its failure kind.
firstReason: Cancelling on log overflow leaves the caller unable to tell which external actions ran, and a retry repeats them. Truncate-and-continue is the safe rule for any program that has side effects.

title: PTC mode — the model writes TypeScript against the tool registry
summary: PTC (programmatic tool calling) is a presentation mode of the tool registry: instead of one schema per tool, the model gets a single `run_code` tool and a generated TypeScript declaration of the tools, and writes a program that calls them. Code execution is a capability seam (`ctx.ptcRuntime`) that knows nothing about tools, and the shipped runtime runs each program in a fresh Node process under the session's sandbox policy.
firstReason: The mode cuts round trips and context use, and its design already puts the program in a separate sandboxed process, so the host language does not matter. The Go host keeps the seam and the control channel; a JavaScript runtime remains an external prerequisite for this mode.

title: Typed tool returns in PTC mode
summary: In PTC mode a tool binding resolves to the tool's final canonical JSON value, and a failed call rejects with a real `ToolCallError`, instead of every result being flattened to one string. The generated declaration gives each tool its real parameter and return types.
firstReason: Programs must not scrape ids out of prose. A canonical JSON output per tool is also what a Go tool returns naturally, and the declaration generator is a deterministic projection of schemas that the Go registry can produce.

title: Tool reachability and initial disclosure
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: describe every tool by two model-facing dimensions, reachability (`native`, `program` or `both`) and initial disclosure (`none`, `name`, `summary` or `full`), in place of the single provider-specific `deferLoading` flag. Every reachable tool stays searchable.
firstReason: Adopt. It gives one vocabulary for native tools, program-only tools and on-demand loading, and the Go tool registry can be designed around it from the start instead of having it added later.

title: Pre-tool input rewrite — a consistent design
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: let a pre-tool hook rewrite a tool call's arguments as a transaction that runs before the call's identity is created, so that the audit event (with the original kept beside it), the derived model history and the UI all show what actually ran. Mutating the frozen execution object is ruled out.
firstReason: Adopt the constraint and defer the feature. The Go loop can place a rewrite phase before the log commit from the start, which upstream cannot do without reordering events; the open question of whether providers accept a rewritten assistant message on replay must be settled first.

title: TypeScript-only PTC tool execution
summary: Programmatic tool calling accepts programs in one language only, TypeScript. Python rendering, language dispatch and Python-specific naming restrictions were removed; the runtime service itself stays independent of tools.
firstReason: Supporting one program language keeps one SDK generator, one set of naming rules and one test matrix. The Go design should also commit to a single language. Inference: TypeScript stays the natural choice because the model writes it, but the Go host then has to run it in a separate runtime process, which the PTC area must specify.

title: Retire the prompt registry change event
summary: Proposal: stop emitting an event when a system-prompt provider is registered or removed, because nothing in the product listens to it; the prompt is rebuilt for every model step anyway.
firstReason: Adopt: the Go system-prompt registry should not publish a change event until a consumer needs one. An advertised event is a public promise with tests and ordering rules to maintain.
